US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there has been “no discussion” of extending the US’ final withdrawal from Iraq, which is slated for the end of this month.
The US military presence in Iraq is scheduled to officially end on September 30 after more than two decades, following a 2024 agreement to withdraw remaining troops after the end of the ISIS campaign.
Still, Baghdad has struggled to deal with the militias within its country. Iranian-backed militia in Iraq have launched waves of strikes on US and allied interests amid the war in Iran.
Rubio, who met with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi at the UN General Assembly on Monday, said al-Zaidi did not ask the US to extend its presence.
President Donald Trump also saw al-Zaidi “briefly” on Tuesday night, Rubio told reporters in New York.
Responding to a question from CNN, Rubio said the US has “zero doubt” of al-Zaidi’s commitment to try to control the Iraqi militias but noted that it is “a massive challenge.”
The top US diplomat said the Iraqi prime minister has “achieved certain things” with regard to the militias, noting that “at least three militias have disarmed and have basically joined the national government.”
“As we’ve told him, we want him to succeed. We think he gives the world and Iraq the best chance to succeed. I think he has the right intentions. I think he has the right motivations. He’s very intelligent and a very willing partner in this regard, and we’re going to do everything we can to help him achieve the results,” he said.
“Nothing would be more important for Iraq than to deal with this and to bring all the arms in that country under the control of the national government,” Rubio added.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that US-Iran talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly were “a continuation of conversations that have occurred in the past,” but not a major breakthrough.
Rubio also appeared to indicate that a return to the Memorandum of understanding (MoU) that was struck between the US and Iran earlier this year was no longer on the cards from the US perspective.
“They killed the MOU, they strangled it,” Rubio said, pointing to the Iranian strikes which led to the temporary ceasefire collapsing in June.
But Rubio refused to characterize the US demands during the meeting with any specificity. The meeting was led on the US side by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio acknowledged the challenge posed by the severe threats to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz but said that US military escorts to keep oil moving through the critical waterway will continue. He once again put emphasis on the overall focus being stopping Iran’s nuclear weapons program, saying that issue is not a political one for Trump.
“The core issue here is that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. We make that point in every interaction with them,” Rubio said.
Rubio reiterated his past position that the Iranians in the negotiations are not always able to make commitments on behalf of the regime.
“The ultimate decision making in Iran lies in the hands of people that are strong believers in Iran, the revolution, and that makes interactions problematic because you can deal with the people that represent Iran, the state, and you can reach agreement on some points, and you can even discuss the potential for agreement on other points,” Rubio said. “But they have to take that back to Iran the revolution, and it’s there where it’s often failed.”
President Donald Trump’s meeting with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez was short but important, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday.
Trump and Rodriguez met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.
Rubio, speaking to reporters in New York, said they discussed economic reforms and the political transition process.
On the economy, the top US diplomat said that “debt structuring” is a key step toward fixing the economy so that there is reinvestment in the country.
Rubio told reporters the political transition process is underway
Rubio said they don’t want someone to be elected and inherit “a complete catastrophe.”
Asked about reports that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was thrice denied entrance to Venezuela, Rubio suggested he was unaware of the specific reports. He noted that Machado is “very brave” and he has known her for a long time, but noted that “there’s like 8 million Venezuelans” who have left that the US wants to be able to return.
As world leaders gather in New York and Washington signals potential diplomatic contacts with Tehran, a senior Iranian security official warned neighboring countries against complying with new US restrictions targeting Iranian airlines.
Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said countries that cooperate with measures limiting Iranian commercial flights could face retaliatory action.
Speaking in an interview with Iran’s semi-official Student News Network (SNN) on Wednesday, Rezaee said countries should refrain from joining Washington’s “adventurism” and avoid imposing restrictions on Iranian commercial flights, passenger services and cargo transit.
“If countries in the region cooperate with air transport sanctions against Iran, the airports and aviation routes of those countries will likewise face closures and disruptions in response,” Rezaee said, according to SNN.
Rezaee also signaled a tougher Iranian position on diplomacy, saying future talks with Washington, as well as any reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, would depend on the United States meeting Tehran’s conditions first.
The remarks come after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Monday that Iranian airlines would effectively be forced to stop operating from September 23 because of secondary sanctions on air service providers.

articles.title_orig: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.title_zh: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.content_orig:
When the Milwaukee Bucks agreed to sign Gary Trent Jr. to a four-year, $64 million deal in July, red flags went up all around the league's office. Days later, reports emerged suggesting the NBA was looking into the signing , though details of the league's probe were scarce.
The league apparently found enough that it decided to launch a full-on investigation , according to The Athletic. The focus of that investigation: whether the Bucks used the contract as a way to circumvent the NBA salary cap.
The league reportedly hired law firm Hecker Fink to perform that investigation.
That particular accusation should sound familiar, as the league just wrapped an investigation on the Los Angeles Clippers and Kawhi Leonard that looked into the exact same thing. While both teams were accused of the same violation, their methods for allegedly circumventing the salary cap differ.
In the Clippers' case, the team was accused of using a team sponsor to funnel additional funds to Leonard as a way to get around NBA rules. Accusations surrounding the Bucks are far more straight forward.
The league is reportedly looking into whether the Bucks made handshake agreements with Trent to sign lesser deals the past two offseasons with the promise of Trent eventually receiving a much larger contract this offseason.
The issue stems from Trent's massive pay increase this offseason. After making $2.6 million with the Bucks in 2024 and $3.7 million in 2025, Trent's new deal will pay him an average of over $15 million the next four years.
That massive pay increase came after Trent experienced a down season, one in which he averaged just 8.1 points per game, his lowest scoring output since his rookie season.
When reached for comment by The Athletic, the NBA, Bucks and Trent's agency — Klutch Sports — all declined comment. Both the Bucks and Klutch are reportedly working with the NBA as it performs its investigation, per The Athletic.
Should the NBA determine the Bucks purposefully engaged in salary-cap circumvention, the team could see a similar punishment to the Clippers. The NBA came down hard on Los Angeles , docking the team five future first-round picks , fining and suspending team owner Steve Ballmer and fining Leonard.

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison Wednesday, more than a year after a jury found the former Hollywood mogul guilty of sexually assaulting former “Project Runway” production assistant Miriam Haley in a high-stakes retrial.
Weinstein, who pleaded not guilty to a charge of first-degree criminal sexual act, appeared in the downtown Manhattan courtroom in a wheelchair, his hands cuffed to his seat.
In a victim impact statement read aloud in the courtroom, Haley said Weinstein “abused his position and power,” causing a “devastating effect on my life and security.”
“It is a life sentence for me,” Haley said.
Weinstein also addressed the court, again denying the allegations against him while apologizing to “anyone I may have hurt by my actions.”
“I am not a perfect person,” he said, “but I am a person who has made mistakes.” He later added: “I am not a violent man.”
Judge Curtis Farber excoriated Weinstein before handing down his sentence. “You took what you wanted by force, and you have never accepted responsibility,” the judge told the former entertainment industry kingmaker.
Farber said Weinstein’s 15-year sentence will be followed by five years of supervised release and a requirement that he register as a sex offender.
Wednesday’s sentencing came after a protracted series of trials, appeals and courtroom proceedings that have kept Weinstein behind bars since his arrest in 2018, one of the key events of the #MeToo movement.
Weinstein was originally convicted in 2020 of third-degree rape involving former aspiring actor Jessica Mann and first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley. He was sentenced to 23 years in prison. But his conviction was overturned in 2024 by a New York state appeals court, and a judge ordered a new trial.
Weinstein was again found guilty in June 2025 of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley, who testified that he forcibly performed oral sex on her in his New York City apartment in 2006. The same jury acquitted him of a separate criminal sex act charge involving allegations from former model Kaja Sokola.
The jurors at Weinstein’s second New York trial could not reach a verdict on the charge related to Mann’s allegation, and a third trial on that charge also ended in a hung jury. In late June, prosecutors declined to try the Mann case a fourth time.
Weinstein was separately convicted in Los Angeles in December 2022 of rape and two counts of sexual assault related to a 2013 assault of an Italian actor and model. He was sentenced by a Los Angeles judge to 16 years in prison in February 2023.
He is set to be resentenced in L.A. after an appeals court vacated his original sentence.
The former producer and film distributor vehemently denies all allegations of sexual misconduct, insisting his sexual encounters were consensual. In all, more than 80 women have accused Weinstein of sexual assault or harassment.
Weinstein once lorded over Hollywood. Miramax, his first distribution label, released seminal independent films like “Clerks” and “Pulp Fiction.” He won an Oscar as a producer of “Shakespeare in Love.” In the early 2010s, his second distribution company scored back-to-back best picture wins for “The King’s Speech” and “The Artist.”
But his reign came crashing down in 2017 after The New York Times and The New Yorker published exposés detailing his alleged pattern of sexual harassment and assault. The first wave of accusations against him in 2017 propelled the #MeToo movement, a reckoning with sexual misconduct by powerful people in high-profile professions.
In recent years, Weinstein’s health has visibly declined, and he has faced various medical issues, including diagnoses of bone marrow cancer, kidney disease and diabetes. He has been held at the Bellevue Hospital prison ward, and he will remain there until he is sent to a state prison.
Daniel Arkin is a senior reporter at NBC News.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.

The East Coast is already beginning to see the impacts of a developing nor'easter , with major coastal flooding set to begin Wednesday night from New Jersey to the Virginia Tidewater. All told, millions from New England to the Carolinas will experience days of coastal flooding, strong winds and pounding surf through the weekend.
The system that will become the first nor'easter of the season is set to emerge off the Mid-Atlantic coast between Thursday and Friday before charging towards the heavily populated Northeast .
TIMELINE: HERE'S WHERE AND WHEN MAJOR US CITIES WILL SEE IMPACTS FROM THE DEVELOPING NOR'EASTER
The coastal flood risk will increase throughout the workweek from North Carolina 's Outer banks to New England as strong northeasterly winds develop across the offshore and coastal waters, producing powerful wind gusts.
Seas will rise rapidly, creating heavy surf and dangerous, battering waves along exposed beaches .
According to the FOX Forecast Center , persistent onshore winds will remain locked in through multiple high tide cycles , allowing waves to relentlessly pound the base of coastal dunes.
OUTER BANKS FIRST IN LINE FOR DEVELOPING NOR’EASTER AS DANGEROUS IMPACTS BEGIN WEDNESDAY
Significant beach erosion and dune scarping will develop from the Outer Banks through the Mid-Atlantic and Long Island as the surface low-pressure system forms.
Minor to locally moderate coastal flooding will be possible during high tides, especially in low-lying coastal areas like Highway 12 in the North Carolina Outer Banks.
Sea rise could be anywhere from 2 to 3 feet, the FOX Forecast Center said.
FULL MOON COULD WORSEN NOR’EASTER FLOODING ALONG EAST COAST — HERE ARE 5 PLACES TO WATCH
Heading into Thursday, things shift as the surface low pressure system centralizes and strengthens off the Southeast coast and onshore winds expand and intensify.
Widespread tidal flooding will be possible as water becomes unable to drain during low tides and gets trapped in back bays and low-lying areas along the coast.
Some places could even see major flooding, with the FOX Forecast Center saying some of the worst flooding could happen in coastal Maryland and Virginia .
Rain and winds are also predicted to become an issue at this point, with wind gusts between 40 and 50 mph in some coastal areas, pushing ocean water inland.
NOR'EASTER LIVE TRACKER: FUTURE RADAR, WINDS, STORM SURGE, RAIN AND ALERTS
Days of these continuous pounding waves will severely impact beaches. Dune washouts, overwashes and damage to oceanfront boardwalks or coastal infrastructure are increasingly likely across Mid-Atlantic and Long Island beaches.
New England should start seeing rain at this stage, with a Level 1 out of 4 flood threat in effect for Boston , and parts of Rhode Island .
Beginning Saturday, the nor'easter really becomes prominent as the center of the low pressure system moves toward the Interstate 95 corridor and New England.
WILL THE MONSTER NOR'EASTER CANCEL YOUR WEEKEND PLANS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW
As the strengthening system tracks into or near New England, the strongest pressure gradient will impact the region, including Boston .
The exact track is still not certain, with some models pushing the low toward Boston, while others show the low pressure closer to New Jersey and Long Island, or even staying offshore. All three scenarios will create more significant impacts in different areas.
If the storm shifts closer to Boston, this could turn the storm into a major weather event, featuring 60 to 70 mph wind gusts, heavy rainfall , major storm surge and significant disruptions to Boston Harbor and the Massachusetts coastline, the FOX Forecast Center said.
If the storm shifts closer to New Jersey or Long Island, the strongest impacts could shift farther south, potentially putting New York City on the fringe of the storm.

Lastly, if the area of low pressure remains offshore, coastal New England could still experience rough surf, elevated tides and breezy conditions, while the heaviest rain and strongest winds remain displaced to the south and east over open water. The FOX Forecast Center said this scenario is the least likely of the three.
THIS NOR’EASTER MAY FOLLOW THE SAME PATH AS SUPERSTORM SANDY, BUT IT’S NOTHING LIKE IT
The FOX Forecast Center said no matter what, winds could gust more than 60 mph as the peak of the storm shifts into southern New England, Massachusetts Bay and the Gulf of Maine .
Dangerous seas, extreme rip currents and massive swells will make ocean waters extremely dangerous.
Rain continues in New England through Sunday. A Level 1 out of 4 flash flood threat stretches from Cape Cod, Rhode Island and coastal Massachusetts, expanding north into parts of New Hampshire. Rain totals will be heaviest along coastal locations.
Impacts are expected to linger through Monday, but as the storm's track becomes more certain, the forecast could change slightly.

articles.title_orig: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Garoppolo and 4 other names for NFL teams in need of a quarterback
articles.title_zh: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Garoppolo and 4 other names for NFL teams in need of a quarterback
articles.content_orig:
The NFL season is only two weeks old, and yet six teams have already dealt with injuries to their starting quarterbacks.
The Falcons were already without Michael Penix Jr. because of his recovery from an ACL injury when Tua Tagovailoa went down with a back injury just days before the opener. In Week 1, the Seahawks lost Sam Darnold to a glute injury and Vikings starter Kyler Murray suffered a concussion. Week 2 was even worse: The Commanders lost Jayden Daniels to another dislocated elbow (the same one he dislocated last season), the Bears watched Caleb Williams get carted off with a hamstring injury and then placed backup Tyler Bagent in the concussion protocol , and the Giants saw Jaxson Dart go down with a knee injury whose severity is still to be determined.
The spate of early injuries to quarterbacks has reinforced the value of experienced (and reliable) backups. The teams that have them have remained competitive; Seattle and Minnesota are both 2-0 with respective backups Drew Lock and Carson Wentz filling in.
But the teams that lack a solid No. 2 or any real depth at the position have paid a price. Just look at Atlanta, where third-stringer Cooper Rush was benched during a blowout loss to the Panthers after throwing his fourth pick of the season. He was replaced by Jack Strand -- who promptly threw a pick-six.
There's good news in store for a few teams. Penix will start for the Falcons on Thursday night and Tagovailoa is back to fully participating in practice. Darnold is expected to return to practice in some capacity this week for the Seahawks and Murray has been cleared from the concussion protocol in Minnesota.
But that leaves three teams who could potentially be in search of reinforcement.
Case Keenum is the only other quarterback on the Bears' active roster and, although he has 66 starts in his 14-year NFL career, he hasn't played a regular-season snap since December 2023.
In Washington, it remains unclear how much time Daniels might miss. X-rays of Daniels' elbow were negative for any fractures, but coach Dan Quinn declined to provide any details about the MRI results. Daniels will not start Sunday against the Seahawks, but how long he'll be out thereafter is unknown. In the meantime, the Commanders will turn to Marcus Mariota , just as they have the last two seasons when Daniels has dealt with injuries. The difference this time around: Washington doesn't have an experienced third-string QB like they did in Josh Johnson last year. The team's current No. 3 is seventh-round rookie Athan Kaliakmanis, a young player who showed some promise in preseason but is still quite green.
The Giants are in a similar if not worse position. Dart could be out for the rest of the season, a much worse outcome than what was originally expected. Jameis Winston is expected to take over as the starter, but he's the only other quarterback on the Giants' active roster. Jake Haener, a fourth-round pick by the Saints in 2023, is on the practice squad.
So who might be available to help?
Finding a quality backup quarterback at this point in the season is difficult, but there are a number of veterans and young QBs who could serve as extra insurance, if not more, for teams in need. From potential trade candidates to street free agents and practice squad players, here are some players who may be under consideration, either now or after the next prominent starter goes down.
The sixth-year quarterback has seemingly found his groove in San Francisco as Brock Purdy's backup. After a standout rookie season with the Patriots in which he was named a Pro Bowl alternate, Jones cycled through multiple play callers and quickly regressed. He was traded to Jacksonville in 2024 and started seven of 10 games in relief of Trevor Lawrence. But it wasn't until he signed a two-year deal with the 49ers in 2025 that he really showed his worth as a reliable backup. He went 5-3 as a fill-in starter, recording a 69.6 completion percentage, averaging 7.4 yards per attempt and compiling a 97.4 passer rating -- all career bests. San Fran may want to hold onto him to spell Purdy, but it could also get a decent return from a desperate team for a player who is set to be a free agent after this season.
The 12-year veteran and two-time Super Bowl winner reportedly considered retirement in the offseason, but ultimately decided to keep his options open in the NFL. Garoppolo, 34,  hasn't had any real playing time since the 2024 season, when he started the Rams' regular-season finale against the Seahawks, and he hasn't had any consistent playing time since the start of the 2023 season, with the Raiders. But he does have a 43-21 record as a starter, to go with a 67.4 career completion percentage and 97.7 passer rating.
Johnson, 40, is in his 19th season of professional football and still going, as a member of the Bengals' practice squad. He is the ultimate journeyman, playing for a record 14 NFL teams. Johnson was Washington's third-string quarterback last season until Daniels went down and he became the backup and then the starter late in the season when Mariota suffered a quad injury. His familiarity with offensive coordinator David Blough and Washington's other quarterbacks could make him a viable option if the Commanders seek outside reinforcement. But Johnson also has deep ties to Giants coach John Harbaugh (and his brother). Johnson had three stints with the Ravens when Harbaugh was their head coach, totaling seven games (one start) and completing 69.8 percent of his passes for 321 passing yards, two TDs, a pick and a 97.1 passer rating.
Levis signed to the Jets' practice squad on Tuesday, so should the Giants be interested in adding him to their active roster, he'd have a pretty easy move. But would they? The 2023 second-round pick by the Titans showed some promise when he took over for Ryan Tannehill as a rookie in 2023. But injuries and poor performances derailed his tenure in Tennessee. He was benched late in the 2024 season, when Giants quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan was Tennessee's head coach. Levis missed all of 2025 because of a shoulder injury and was released last month after losing the backup job to Mitchell Trubisky.
Richardson never developed into the franchise quarterback the Colts hoped he'd be when they drafted him fourth overall in 2023. Injuries, performance issues and general readiness questions after he tapped out for a play during a narrow loss to the Texans in '24 put him on the outs with the organization. He lost his starting job to Daniel Jones, requested a trade and is now in the final year of his rookie contract (the Colts declined his fifth-year option). If Richardson is viewed as more of a developmental project, then a team in need of immediate help may be unlikely to trade for him. But never say never.
The same context holds for McCarthy, the Vikings' 2024 first-round pick. McCarthy missed the entirety of his rookie season because of a torn meniscus and was sidelined for seven games last season because of injuries. McCarthy fell to third string this season after the team signed Murray to start and re-signed Wentz as his backup. McCarthy has started only 10 games and has more interceptions (12) than touchdowns (11). But he's well-liked in the Harbaugh family. John Harbaugh's brother, Jim, once lauded McCarthy as the greatest quarterback in Michigan history.
The 10-year veteran has spent more than four seasons with Callahan: three in Cincinnati, when Callahan was the Bengals' coordinator; another in Tennessee, when Callahan was head coach, and this offseason with the Giants. Allen was among the roster cuts late last month.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow off 125 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq fall as 10-year Treasury yield surges to highest since 2007 and oil prices rise
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow off 125 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq fall as 10-year Treasury yield surges to highest since 2007 and oil prices rise
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities fell on Wednesday as Treasury yields marched higher amid concerns among investors that more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve may be coming down the pike.
The S&P 500 dropped 0.6%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 313 points, or 0.6%.
Declines in utilities, consumer discretionary and communication services stocks led the broader market's fall, with the three sectors shedding more than 1% each.
Equities were weighed down by an increase in Treasury yields, which jumped after the latest purchasing managers' index readings came in hot . The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.087%, its highest level since July 2007, while the 2-year Treasury note yield hit its highest level since June 2024 at 4.887%.
"We have a lot of strength in corporate earnings, but we also have this inflationary pressure, and there's a tug of war there," Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon, said to CNBC, adding that it's "not just oil" that's driving inflation.
"It's broader, and it's particularly in the services sector," he said. "There's no way that the Fed is going to lower rates or pause at this point. Probably we're going to see maybe two, three rate increases."
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday that "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to get inflation under control.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way," he said. "Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded."
Odds that the Fed would hike rates by a quarter percentage point in October stood above 73% following the developments, according to the CME FedWatch tool . That's up from 55.4% a day ago and just 8.8% one month ago.
Crude oil futures moved up as well. Brent crude futures for November delivery were last seen trading 3% higher at around $102 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were up 2% at around $92 per barrel.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours during the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
In Tuesday's session, the Nasdaq hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record, while the Dow finished lower. The S&P 500 was roughly flat, though the index is about 0.8% off from its all-time high.
McDonald's shares fell sharply Wednesday as the company unveiled a new multiyear growth plan alongside a warning from the company that high inflation and flat restaurant traffic are likely to persist.
CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC that the company is "not expecting things to change" as elevated costs and sluggish traffic continue to weigh on the industry.

An ICE agent who shot a Venezuelan DoorDash driver in Texas was a recruit and was not wearing a body camera at the time, according to multiple reports.
​Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez , 28, was shot once in Austin, Texas, Sunday while carrying out his deliveries. The Austin Police Department, which responded to the shooting, has now released footage taken during Garcés Pérez’s arrest.
​However, three officials at the Department of Homeland Security told The Atlantic that the ICE agent who shot the 28-year-old was not wearing his body camera and was hired last year. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are required to switch on their cameras before enforcement actions take place and may only stop recording once the incident has concluded.
​The sources did not name the agent to The Atlantic , but confirmed that he has previously worked with a different federal law enforcement agency.
Officials told NBC News that the agent had been issued a body camera but that he was not wearing it.
“Before we hear anything from ICE about ‘we pulled him over’ or ‘he was fleeing’ or ‘he was aggressive,’” Garcés Pérez’s attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, wrote on X , “our response to any statements like this is: ‘We won’t believe you until you show us...show us your body cam footage, show us your dash cam footage.
“Otherwise nobody believes you.”
​One of the unnamed officials told The Atlantic the shooting was preceded by ICE agents trying to pull the 28-year-old’s vehicle over, with Garcés Pérez allegedly driving away - allegedly almost striking an officer in the process. The sources said the moment was captured on a second ICE agent’s body camera.
​The agents tried to detain Garcés Pérez , but the Venezuelan man began driving away once again. That was when the officer opened fire, the sources say.
​During a press conference, Garcés Pérez shared his own account of the incident by phone and via a translator. He claimed that he performed a U-turn and was trying to park when officers rammed his car and shot him in the back of the neck.
​Lincoln-Goldfinch said the bullet still remains in her client’s body and that he had to be transferred back to the hospital from the ICE facility, after he began to experience difficulty in lifting his arm.
The attorney also said her client lawfully entered the U.S. after being inspected by Customs and Border Protection and issued a work permit. The Department of Homeland Security claimed his work permit expired in 2025.
Garcés Pérez’s deportation order was issued in absentia because the hearing notice was sent to the wrong address, Lincoln-Goldfinch said .
​DoorDash told NBC News that it is conducting an investigation into the shooting.
​This is the latest in a series of similar incidents involving ICE agents, following the fatal shooting of a Mexican native Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by an ICE officer in Houston two months ago. The DHS said Salgado Araujo rammed an ICE vehicle and “weaponized his vehicle” in an attempt to run over an agent.
Crackdowns on immigration have been a centerpiece of President Donald Trump’s domestic policy. Government data analyzed by The Associated Press and published by the Deportation Data Project stated that ICE made 49,571 arrests in July alone.
At the start of the year, the DHS stated that it had received 220,000 applications to join ICE and that it had 12,000 new agents operating across the country.
The Independent has contacted the DHS and DoorDash for comment.

articles.title_orig: Greetings from Edinburgh, where a cheeky tour guide makes art history hilarious
articles.title_zh: Greetings from Edinburgh, where a cheeky tour guide makes art history hilarious
articles.content_orig:
Growing up, I had a knack for getting distracted on school field trips to museums and art galleries.
Teachers marched us through halls of what felt like the same Baroque painting over and over. Endless soft bodies painted against pale blue skies, their stories offered up with little explanation.
It didn't feel like any of it was meant to be fun.
Then I discovered Coco, the self-described "time-traveling tart."
The brainchild and alter ego of comedian Max Norman, Coco — 6 foot 7 without heels — leads interactive and (mostly) factual tours through galleries in London and beyond.
During the Edinburgh Fringe Festival last month, she made her way to the National Galleries of Scotland for what was billed as a "cheeky romp" uncovering the "gossip, glamour and glorious absurdity hiding behind the art."
Coco had us curtsy before paintings of kings and queens of Great Britain's past, then treated us to lessons about the indulgences and insecurities that made them feel all too human.
We played dead on the floor in a lesson about the fall of the Jacobites in 18th century Scotland (let's just say swords are no match for guns).
Then we all eagerly galloped like horses from one gallery room to the next. I do not remember why — which may have been the point.
Norman created Coco as "revenge" on his artist mother, who used to drag him through art galleries across London.
For anyone who spent their own childhood staring blankly at an Old Master while waiting for someone (anyone!) to make it interesting, Coco feels less like revenge — and more like justice.

articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats
articles.content_orig:
Bryan Seaver, who announced Parton’s death to the world, is alleged to have intimidated her manager and others, which he denies
The estate of the late Dolly Parton is involved in a dispute with the country star’s nephew and former head of security, and has filed for a restraining order against him amid allegations of threats.
Bryan Seaver was responsible for Parton’s security, and was tasked with announcing her death on 25 August with a video, “something Dolly asked of me years ago”, he said.
But since the singer died, her estate, which is run by Parton’s manager Danny Nozell, has reportedly fired Seaver from his security job, and has now alleged that he made “relentless” threats against Nozell and others.
According to Billboard, the lawsuit filed in a Tennessee court reads: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”
Seaver is alleged to have written to a lawyer for Parton, “I’m a killer”, and separately told Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” He is also alleged to have claimed that he made a $27m arms and ammunition deal with Haiti.
He allegedly claimed he would “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”
Seaver repeated some of those claims in comments to TMZ while defending his actions, saying: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”
Regarding the messages to Nozell, Seaver said: “I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”
In another message, Seaver reportedly said: “I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”
Speaking to TMZ, Seaver said of that comment: “I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.”
Seaver’s security contract was terminated on 15 September, with a leaked termination letter saying the decision was made “for the protection of the trust and beneficiaries as a whole”, though it reassured Seaver it was “not a termination of your personal interest in the trust”.
Seaver put out a statement after the termination, saying: “We remain unshakably resolved to fulfil her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.”
The chancery court in Nashville will now consider the restraining order filing. The Guardian has contacted Seaver and lawyers for Parton’s estate for further comment.
Parton left behind considerable financial assets: not only her songbook featuring hits such as 9 to 5, but also a broad business empire including the entertainment resort Dollywood in Tennessee.
She had no children, and her husband, Carl, died in 2025, but she is survived by other family members including six siblings and an uncle. Seaver is the son of her sister Cassie.

articles.title_orig: China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington on Wednesday with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
articles.title_zh: China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington on Wednesday with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump wants the U.S. to beat China in the artificial intelligence race. But as he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping , both countries are also weighing how to address the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology.
In recent months, AI systems have taken more consequential actions online: OpenAI said one of its research models gained unauthorized access to parts of the AI platform Hugging Face, while Anthropic found AI was being used to automate parts of cyberattacks. The incidents have raised fears that increasingly autonomous models could make attacks faster and harder to contain.
Ahead of Trump and Xi's meeting on Thursday, U.S. Treasury Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, over the weekend, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level."
"Leaders in both countries are spooked by the increasing cyber capabilities of AI models, and especially agents acting autonomously to escape containment and breach websites," Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC.
But as fears have intensified, tensions have not dissipated.
Washington continues to restrict China's access to Nvidia 's most advanced AI chips and has accused Chinese AI companies of using "distillation" — training models on the output of more advanced U.S. systems — a claim Beijing rejects.
While the U.S. took an early lead in developing large language models, or LLMs, thanks to companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, Chinese models have made big capability gains in recent months and are increasingly being adopted by companies globally, including in America.
Trump previously dismissed warnings that AI poses an existential threat to humanity, risks amplified by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic chief Dario Amodei as they called for an industry slowdown and regulatory oversight.
"If we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position," Trump told reporters earlier this month.
But in a Truth Social post Monday, he said the government "will rein things in if we have to."
Some lawmakers hopeful that the talks will result in some sort of agreement on AI, while being realistic that the summit may be more about the fact it's happening than deliverables.
"I hope Trump meets with Xi Jinping and comes up with some common sense safeguards," Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., who represents part of Silicon Valley, said in an interview Wednesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box."
"How about we just agree that you should not be able to have self-improving AI?" Khanna said. "Why wouldn't you want to sit down with Xi Jinping and say let's have some reasonable agreement? And have it enforceable, trust but verify."
The likeliest areas of agreement between the U.S. and China could be common definitions and frameworks for AI safety for powerful models and an emergency communication mechanism to discuss incidents, Mehta told CNBC.
A channel for relating national security-related incidents would be a "modest" but positive step, Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.
But an agreement to slow down AI's breakneck development speed is "extremely unlikely," he added.
China has historically used AI dialogues "to complain about U.S. export controls," McGuire said, which the U.S. uses to prevent the most advanced AI chips from being sold to China.
"Its state media has largely rejected the concerns expressed by leading U.S. AI labs about the potential for catastrophic risk, which is consistent with China's long-held skepticism of all U.S. arms control proposals," he added.
Despite U.S. restrictions, several Chinese firms have reportedly been able to access the chips' compute power remotely, via data centers in Southeast Asia.
While U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said controls on chips were not on the agenda during preliminary talks on the weekend, China could push to have them relaxed, said Melanie Hart, senior director of the think tank Atlantic Council's Global China Hub.
"China's asking the U.S. to embrace Chinese AI models and drop some of the U.S. controls on China's access to semiconductor chips," she told reporters on Tuesday.
Distillation could also come up in the talks. U.S. companies and officials have accused Chinese labs of using the practice to gain ground, characterizing it as theft; China rejects the allegations.
In July, Bessent threatened sanctions against companies doing it and said the Trump administration had found "watermarks of our U.S. large language models on many of the Chinese models," calling it "unacceptable."
Progress on AI cooperation relies on two things, said Mehta. "The first is that it can't hurt the ability for the U.S. and China to compete on the merits of their technology."
The second is a verification mechanism, he added. "Policymakers won't be inclined to take their counterparts just on their word, so we'll need to find ways to ensure information flowing between the two countries is accurate. That means both technical and governance verification tools."

CHICAGO, IL — McDonald's ( MCD ) is making a long-term bet on artificial intelligence, hand-breaded chicken, and a return of 90s-style restaurants to regain customers who left for other chains, like Burger King.
At its investor day in Chicago, the fast food giant unveiled a new set of ambitious goals and investments as part of its growth plan , following a rocky second quarter that resulted in 0.8% US same-store sales growth versus Burger King's whopping 8.5% growth.
McDonald's said it plans to invest $8.5 billion through 2036 to support restaurant tech updates with rent relief and capital. It intends to deliver roughly $5 billion of that investment by 2030.
Franchisees are encouraged to adopt the plan in phases. One franchisee operator told Yahoo Finance they are skating on thin margins with higher ingredient, labor, and rent costs, making another costly redesign difficult, especially in a high-interest-rate environment.
Deploying the entire NEXT strategy will cost franchise operators an additional $800,000 per restaurant. Operators are expected to update the restaurants' look and feel as part of a remodel cycle every 10 years, per McDonald's.
"You start with the opportunity, which we think is really clear and compelling," McDonald's CFO Ian Borden told Yahoo Finance. "We think it's going to provide a really strong return for our operators and for McDonald's."
It remains to be seen whether the strategic growth plan can turn around McDonald's stock . McDonald's shares have struggled to entice investors to take a bite this year, declining 18% year to date, compared to a 4.6% gain for Burger King's parent company stock, Restaurant Brands International ( QSR ), and 13% gain for the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).
McDonald's stock fell 5% on Wednesday.
Part of the strategy is a commitment called "Make it Golden," which doubles down on food, hospitality, and employee training.
After Burger King overhauled its chicken nugget recipe, McDonald's is doing something similar by piloting hand-breaded chicken.
The chicken comes frozen, marinated, dipped in batter, and hand-breaded, Jacques Mignault, McDonald's Global Chief Restaurant Officer, told Yahoo Finance. The secret is to flip the chicken seven times.
McDonald's is targeting a 1.5% gain in market share, with the chicken and beverage categories leading the way ( crafted sodas are another major focus for McDonald's). It expects to add more US restaurants to the hand-breaded chicken pilot in early 2027.
Mignault said the new chicken is "actually beating the competition from a taste and quality standpoint" in Asian markets. He added that the company has also started testing bone-in wings.
McDonalds also aims to maintain its beef market share leadership after leaning into the Big Arch Bu rger , which went viral earlier this year after a video of CEO Chris Kempczinski tasting the burger prompted other fast food CEOs to respond.
Gone is the modernized, gray box design McDonald's implemented years ago.
Now, McDonald's is reintroducing a smaller PlayPlace, featuring a slide, jungle gym, and analog toys (no, there's no ball pit).
The goal is for families to visit restaurants more often and spend more when they do. Foot traffic at McDonald's has faltered. During the week of Sept. 7, McDonald's foot traffic fell 3.1% year over year, compared to a 2.8% decline in overall quick-service restaurants and a 7.1% gain for Burger King, per Placer.ai.
"Our customers were telling us, look, McDonald's used to be fun, just inject some of the personality back into the look and feel of restaurants," Jill McDonald, executive vice president and global chief restaurant experience officer, told Yahoo Finance.
The back of the house is also getting an upgrade with AI technology, dubbed ArchIQ.
Think kitchens and drive-throughs integrated with artificial intelligence, powered by Google Edge ( GOOG ). Even artificial intelligence will be used to ensure the McFlurry Machine does not go down.
CFO Borden said this is different than the company's previous partnership with IBM ( IBM ), which ended in 2024.
"A few years ago, it was a different technology platform," Borden said. "That large language model that we are building with Google just allows the learning to get sharper and sharper. … We are already far advanced versus where we were several years ago with what we were doing previously."
The use of AI technology is a game changer, executives say, and will contribute to a part of a 250 basis point improvement in gross restaurant-level efficiency gains, which the company said is equivalent to roughly $100,000 in annual cash flow for the average US restaurant.
The drive-through technology is expected to save restaurants' 50-plus labor hours per week, McDonald's said.

US-Iran meeting takes place on sidelines despite president’s threat to ‘annihilate’ Tehran regime. Plus, one man’s month-long pilates odyssey
Good morning. Donald Trump has used the platform of the UN general assembly in New York to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran, “and do it quickly”. He called on countries to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices.
Despite his bombastic rhetoric, Trump also said Iranian officials held three hours of talks with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the meeting. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June. A senior Iranian official also indicated that Iran was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week.
What else did Trump say at the UN? The president doubled down on his defence of AI development, saying warnings about runaway agents were a “hoax”; announced the US would build new military bases in Greenland; attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation”; and prompted the Cuba’s delegation to stage a walkout when he described the country as a “failed state”.
Did he continue his attacks on US media networks ? Trump scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN, saying “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Last week, the president announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House.

John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”.
Where else is the president seeing dissent from Republicans? Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Trump , days after María Elvira Salazar called out the president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump.

Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the 18-year-old’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who did not return from the trip that day.

Medical examiners said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach when she died on August 16.
Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. After her death, her father released a statement, saying: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”

articles.title_zh: Meta's Muse reignites AI disruption fears. Traders are targeting this brokerage stock as next casualty
articles.content_orig:
Meta's latest consumer AI product is sending such big shockwaves through the market that it's even inflaming a long-time rivalry in the brokerage business between 55-year old investing giant Charles Schwab , and Robinhood , an icon of the post-Covid trading boom among young investors. Shares of Schwab fell 6% Tuesday, touching the lowest since early July and the stock is now down more than 8% since Meta announced Muse. Meanwhile, Robinhood's stock was higher, notching anotheryear-to-date high. In May, the company launched AI agents that can now trade and manage portfolios on behalf of users. Shares of sprawling wealth management business LPL Financial Holdings dropped 7% Tuesday, financial services firm Raymond James Financial shed 3.5 percent, and Interactive Brokers slipped 1% as the State Street Financial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLF) lost 2% and is now down 6 percent from highs made earlier this month. Higher interest rates may not be helping. It's not the first time an AI product has jostled the group – in February, the same group of stocks dropped when tech platform Altruist said its platform `Hazel' can create tax-planning strategies for individuals and advisors. Schwab stock recovered some in the months after – LPL has not. "Schwab's an interesting animal," said Jimmy Lee, founder and CEO of The Wealth Consulting Group, a Las Vegas-based advisor that oversees $8 billion in assets. "To us in the advisor space they're kind of neutral and figuring out how best to protect their market share. I don't think Meta brings a lot of competition from the custodian perspective because it's not like Altruist's platform, but there is a lot of disruption that's going to happen among financial middle-men that charge fees for billing, reporting, trading, etc." Meta's AI assistant says it won't trade for users or give financial advice, but when queried with how it might mimic the work of a financial advisor or broker, lists abilities including tracking investments and progress towards goals, as well as analyzing how portfolio holdings fit together.
Last week, Schwab Advisor Services, the company's platform for registered investment advisors, announced it is working with Anthropic to create Claude for Financial Advisors. In May, the company launched an AI tool that includes tailored analysis from the company's research arm. Representatives from Schwab did not respond to a request for comment. Robinhood reps declined to add to this story. Robinhood's bounce on Tuesday brings its stock to a 10% rally on the year after dropping more than 40% in the first three months. The retail-focused brokerage, which also offers digital banking and advisory services, is up 1200 percent the past three years. Schwab stock is up 83 percent and the XLF is up 65 percent. "AI and tokenization threaten to dismantle the frictions that legacy financial intermediaries have historically monetized," Piper Sandler analyst Patrick Moley wrote in a note in April. "Schwab's reliance on low-yielding sweep cash puts it squarely in the crosshairs."
Judging by options-market flows around the stocks on Tuesday, the threat to Schwab may be a lasting one. Options volume in Schwab was more than five times the average, with nearly twice as many puts bought vs. calls, Cboe LiveVol data show. The most popular contract to buy was the 90-strike put expiring mid-January, a bet the stock drops another 13% the next three months. To be sure, there was one big counter-trade sale of the Oct. 16 95-strike puts.
What's arguably most notable is in Robinhood options, sentiment was the opposite – traders bought twice as many calls as puts with more than 80 percent of the $95 million in premium traded tied to calls. The most heavily traded contract was the 125-strike call expiring on Friday. "Gen Z and millennials gravitate towards platforms like Robinhood and Public which is why those platforms ship products so quickly," Gav Blaxberg, founder of Wolf Financial, a popular online trader enclave, said in a call. "Robinhood has built enough trust rebuilding its brand since GameStop and they're allowing agents to trade literally everything."

articles.title_orig: Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
articles.title_zh: Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
articles.content_orig:
The Nepali Army conducts a search-and-rescue operation on Sept. 10 inside the Chilime Hydropower Station tunnel days after the deadly flash floods and mudslides in Nepal's Rasuwa district in August. In the wake of the disaster, concerns are being raised about the impact of the construction of hydropower plants and dams in the Himalayas. Skanda Gautam/AFP/via Getty Images hide caption
KATHMANDU, Nepal — On a recent September day, Sumana Shrestha Amatya stood alongside other protesters in the Nepali capital, urging the government to work faster to find their loved ones, trapped inside hydropower plants since flash floods devastated miles of a river valley in late August.
Amatya says she hasn't heard from officials about her husband, Sunil, a geologist. Still, she acknowledged the scale of the disaster that the government was grappling with: "It was like a Himalayan tsunami."
It's a description other Nepalis have used for the events of Aug. 26, when a glacier and its bedrock spanning more than 3,800 feet in width collapsed into a river valley, some 4,000 feet below.
That triggered 30-foot-high waves of boulders, water and ice that surged for miles downstream. It swept away a multistory border building and some 70 bridges and miles of highway, and buried 12 hydropower plants under mud and boulders along the Trishuli River, which was badly impacted by the floods.
Some 1,400 bodies have been recovered in Nepal , and more than 5,000 remain unaccounted for.
The dead and missing include 121 people who were trapped in hydropower plants, according to Brig. Gen. Subas Jung Thapa of the Nepali army, which is leading rescue efforts. He spoke in early September.
It took days just to find the power plants under the mud. It was like "a bomb's gone off," said Arnold Dix , a tunneling expert helping with rescue efforts. "It's removed the power stations from the surface, like they're just not there." Only three men were found alive in the plants since rescue efforts began.
It is those hydropower plants that have received the most scrutiny in regional media since the floods, with experts reviving questions about whether developers had properly assessed the risks of building them in the Himalayas.
"We need to understand what is happening now in Nepal can happen in other parts of the Himalayas," says C.P. Rajendran , an Indian geoscientist who has been critical of big construction works in the Himalayas. (Rajendran, like many Indians, uses initials for his first name.)
Critics have also focused on the role of international institutions like the World Bank, which has long supported some of these hydropower projects and their associated dams .
They include one of the biggest hydropower projects in the river basin, known as the Upper Trishuli-1, which cost Nepal over half a billion dollars. It was backed by about $300 million in loans and equity by two arms of the World Bank .
The Upper-Trishuli-1 was under construction. Now it's under the mud. Thapa of the Nepali army said in his press briefing that he estimated some 50 people were trapped inside. On Wednesday, the Kathmandu Post reported the bodies of five men were recovered from the plant.
"Why did it have to happen in the first place?" asked Parineeta Dandekar , an expert on rivers who has written critically about these projects for the advocacy group South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People .
Dandekar accuses the World Bank of producing a flawed risk assessment report for the project from the get-go. Its many omissions, Dandekar says, included ignoring "the cumulative disaster risk that can happen after having so many projects across the same river."
Experts say the Trishuli river basin has 36 hydro power projects — including the dozen now under the mud.
Dandekar says the constant blasting of mountains to build these projects, including for miles-long tunnels, has its own impact.
It's a region where earthquakes and landslides are common, and where climate change is causing its glaciers to melt more rapidly, making them — and their slopes — more unstable. Initial analysis suggests global warming exacerbated the melting of the glacier that snapped off in August, triggering flash floods.
There's no clear evidence that the construction of these projects had a role in causing the severity of the Aug. 26 disaster. But experts like geoscientist Rajendran say construction has caused damage in other communities where hydropower projects are being built, including damaging mountain springs, causing homes to crack and even landslides.
In this case, though, says Dipak Gyawali , a hydropower engineer with the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology, "compared to the tectonic forces at play that caused this event, dynamiting is minuscule. This is almost nothing. It's like scratching your skin."
But he and other experts said developers were not seriously investigating the risk caused by so many projects built in the same zone. "These risks have to be properly studied and assessed. Unfortunately, they have not been," Gyawali said.
Retired Indian ambassador Shyam Saran, who served as the Indian prime minister's special envoy for climate change, says developers typically look at risks that could be triggered by their project, alongside environmental risks to it, and they appear safe. "But if you do actually a cumulative environmental impact assessment of the whole river system," he says, "then a different picture emerges."
And the Trishuli river "is a really high-risk area to build [hydropower] dams, says Austin Lord of the Stimson Center, who works on disaster risk reduction in the Himalayan region at the Stimson Center. In events exacerbated by climate change, there's been deadly flooding three years in a row in the Trishuli basin. In 2024 , it was extreme rainfall. In 2025 , a glacial lake burst. This year, a glacier snapped off.
Days before the August flood , Lord and others authored a paper warning that the area was particularly vulnerable to glacial lakes bursting . "Recurring landslides, and prolonged closures," they wrote, "had all highlighted its vulnerability."
In a statement, the World Bank told NPR that the hydropower plant's design reflected assessments that looked at the risk of flooding and landslides using evidence available when the assessment was made in 2018 . The statement said that as more information becomes available about the August floods, "the World Bank Group will consider any implications for risk assessment, monitoring, early warning and emergency response measures in hydropower projects."
Another major funder for the Upper Trishuli-1 was the Asian Development Bank, which loaned $60 million for the project. In 2024, independent experts who visited the site reported that no climate resilience assessment was undertaken. They described that as a "significant gap." The bank did not immediately respond to NPR's question as to whether that assessment was ultimately undertaken.
Arnold Dix, the tunneling expert, defended the hydropower plants' construction. "They were built properly to start with," he said, noting the underground infrastructure, including tunnels, was still intact. He said the collapsing glacier that triggered the August flash floods was an unforeseen new threat that "will change the way we do the designs of the power station."
Advocates say they hope this devastating flood might prompt a rethink of how hydropower is constructed across the Himalayas. Reuters reported in 2025 that China and India, the world's most populous countries, have built 68 major dams in the Himalayas and another 101 are in the pipeline.
Most prominently, China is constructing one of the world's largest dams and hydropower plants in Tibet, costing around $170 billion. It's estimated that it will provide power to 300 million people.

articles.title_orig: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
articles.title_zh: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.
The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban , ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access.
The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing.
It contends that the three news outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ attorney Michael Velchik.
The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes. The letters cite a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.”
The letters also mention news stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia.
The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims.
The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say.
Rubio defends White House media outlet ban
The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post , where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.”
He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated.
First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.
The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds.
Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN.
On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” ​let journalists from CNN, ⁠MS ​NOW and ​Politico back into the White ​House if ​a court rules ‌against ⁠his decision to ban the ​media ​outlets ⁠from the White ​House grounds.
Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins : “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual.
The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities.
Pool coverage is a decades-old system in which one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.
Print and radio pools are still in place, and TV pools for events for other parts of the administration will continue. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities.
Gary Grumbach is an NBC News legal affairs reporter, based in Washington, D.C.
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.

articles.title_orig: Powerful El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths, scientists say
articles.title_zh: Powerful El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths, scientists say
articles.content_orig:
More than 450,000 people are projected to die from additional heat due to the unusually strong El Nino event over the next six months, according to a research report.
The projection, published on Wednesday by the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, runs to February 2027 and compares estimates of heat-related deaths that could be attributed to El Nino with the level expected in a typical year.
Researchers estimate that global land temperatures could climb by about 1.2 degrees Celsius (2.1 degrees Fahrenheit), with extremely hot days 44 percent more frequent than in an average year.
Developing nations and Africa’s Sahel region are expected to be hit disproportionately hard.
The report projected about 66,800 additional deaths across the Sahel, with Nigeria having the highest projected toll of any single country at 31,400, ahead of Indonesia at 19,300 and Sudan at 17,600.
Elsewhere, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia are forecast to see a combined 19,400 extra deaths, with 15,800 projected in India and 13,300 in Brazil.
Michael Greenstone, cofounder of the lab and co-author of the study, said the findings show heat poses the greatest threat where temperatures are already high and incomes relatively low.
“If you’re already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous,” he said.
Richer places tend to have better access to air conditioning, steady water supplies and health services, he added.
Greenstone said the heat risk was likely to outlast the El Nino itself, with repercussions stretching into next summer.
Abhiyant Tiwari, who specialises in heat at NRDC India, told The Associated Press news agency that the projections should spur action.
Funding and delivery remain weak points, he said, even in India, which has sound plans on paper.
“The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths,” he said.
This year’s El Nino began developing in June and is expected to be one of the strongest ever. Experts say the natural weather pattern, which occurs cyclically, is being “supercharged” by climate change .
In early September, the United Nations’ weather agency reported a 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027. But researchers say its dangers could linger into mid-2027.

articles.title_orig: EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
articles.title_zh: EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
articles.content_orig:
The European Union on Tuesday reached a compromise to prolong sanctions for around 3,000 Russian individuals, entities and companies — but it also resulted in the lifting of sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman .
It all comes after lengthy negotiations ahead of a Wednesday deadline to extend the sanctions, which required unanimity among EU countries to be approved.
"The compromise will involve an extension of the regime for 36 months, until 22 September 2029," a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, said.
"The decision was also taken to delist certain individuals under the regime," it added.
Previously, the sanctions were subject to six-month extensions, so Tuesday's agreement allows the EU to avoid another squabble over the sanctions for three years.
Ukraine denounced the EU's removal of oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman from its Russia sanctions list as "shameful and unjustifiable."
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.
"Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor's entourage," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
Zelenskyy did say he was "grateful" to EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for "her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions list".
Kyiv has called on EU countries to impose "national" sanctions on the two oligarchs.
France was one of the countries demanding the removal of Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov from the sanctions list.
Officials in Paris explained the decision as having to do with "national security" concerns. The French government has not provided any additional details.
According to AFP, diplomatic sources say the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan, whose regime is close to Usmanov.
Meanwhile, Fridman's sanctions exemption was put forth by Luxembourg.
Sources say the move comes as Fridman sues Luxembourg for €15 billion ($17 billion) over his frozen assets, due to EU sanctions.
Usmanov and Fridman are two of Russia's best-known oligarchs, and both have a net worth of $14 billion and 16 billion, respectively. They both are known to have close ties to Vladimir Putin.
The Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom. He currently owns the USM holding company, as well as MegaFon, one of Russia's main mobile phone operators.
For his part, Fridman, has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group, which includes Alfa Bank, Russia's largest and most important private commercial bank.
Fridman also co-founded investment firm LetterOne in Luxembourg and stepped down from its board of directors in 2022 after being targeted by European Union sanctions.

articles.title_orig: Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
articles.title_zh: Discord re-launches age verification following backlash over privacy concerns
articles.content_orig:
Discord has re-launched its age verification process for all users, introducing alternative methods that do not require video selfies or ID.
In an update posted yesterday , Discord co-founder and chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy stated that users can verify their age using credit cards, the Apple App Store, Google Play Store, Google Wallet, or AgeKey (which does not share personal or private data).
"By launching a global approach with non-biometric options, we're getting ahead of laws that might ask us to implement something less privacy-focused," said Vishnevskiy.
"The decisions policymakers make now will shape how platforms advance both teen safety and privacy for years to come, and I encourage people to make their perspectives heard where they live."
In February, Discord announced that age verification would be required for all users starting in March.
The rollout was postponed to the second half of 2026 due to privacy concerns. At the time, Vishnevskiy acknowledged that Discord "should have provided more detail about [its] intentions and how the process works."
In its latest update, Discord said it would "publicly document every third-party age assurance vendor and make it clear who each vendor is," which it has done since and can be accessed here .
Discord has also published its age group estimation methodology and released its first age assurance data in the 2026 Transparency Report , which includes information from the UK and Australia launches.
"Previously, I said trust is earned through actions, not posts," said Vishnevskiy. "This launch is where you hold us to that. We'll get some things wrong, but you can judge us on how we respond: how accurate the age group estimation gets, how fast we fix bad calls, and whether we keep publishing the data so you don't have to take my word for it. That's how we earn your trust."
Discord's age verification automatically assigns users to an age group based on account age or associated servers. It does not review messages, calls, or other content.
There are three age groups: Adult (18+), Teen (13 to 17), and Unconfirmed.
New accounts are automatically unconfirmed until Discord has enough data to determine an age group. Users who do not verify their age can continue to use Discord with limitations while the platform determines a group to place them in, though they can verify their age in user settings.
